overview.title: Vector addition as translation; geometric operations as tensor operations
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: Figures 2.6–2.9 illustrate a vector as a point and an arrow, the sum of two vectors, and translation of a whole object; the text states that elementary geometric operations (translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, …) are expressible as tensor operations, starting with translation = vector addition.
overview.central_idea: Adding a vector B to a point A copies A to a new location at a distance and direction given by B; applied to every point of an object, this is a translation — moving without distortion. All elementary geometric operations can be written as tensor operations.
overview.importance: This page turns the abstract 'tensor addition' into a picture that will be reused for every layer in the book: the bias term of a Dense layer is a translation. The list begun here (translation, then rotation, scaling, linear and affine transforms on p.61) culminates in recognising the Dense layer as an affine transform.
learning_objectives: Describe what figures 2.6, 2.7 and 2.8 show about A = [0.5, 1], B = [1, 0.25] and their sum.
Explain why adding the same vector to all points of an object is a translation that does not distort the object.
State that translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, etc. can be expressed as tensor operations.
Read figure 2.9's label [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor] + [x, y] as the translation formula.

summary:
The top of the page holds **figure 2.6** (the point A = [0.5, 1] marked in a 2-D coordinate system) and **figure 2.7** (the same A drawn as an arrow from the origin). To the right of the text, **figure 2.8** shows A, B and A + B: B is drawn both from the origin and chained from the head of A, and A is also chained from the head of B, so the two routes form a parallelogram whose far corner is A + B.

The body text completes the sentence begun on p.59: adding B to A copies point A to a new location whose *distance and direction* from A are determined by B. If the same vector addition is applied to a group of points in the plane — an "object" — you create a copy of the entire object in a new location (**figure 2.9**). Tensor addition therefore represents *translating an object*: moving it without distorting it, by a certain amount in a certain direction.

The authors then generalise: elementary geometric operations such as translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, and so on, can all be expressed as tensor operations. A list of examples begins with **Translation** — adding a vector to a point moves it by a fixed amount in a fixed direction; applied to a set of points (a 2-D object) this is called a translation. Figure 2.9 shows a red square containing the letter K shifted right and up, annotated with `[horizontal_factor, vertical_factor] + [x, y]`: every point `[x, y]` of the K receives the same displacement vector. The list continues on p.61 with rotation, scaling, linear transforms and affine transforms, ending with the observation that `y = W @ x + b` — the Dense layer — is an affine transform.

paragraphs.excerpt: new location, whose distance and direction from the original point A is determined
paragraphs.what_it_says: Completing the p.59 sentence: adding B to A copies A to a new location whose distance and direction from A are given by B. Applying the same addition to a group of points (an 'object') copies the whole object to a new location (figure 2.9). Tensor addition thus represents translating an object — moving it without distorting it — by a certain amount in a certain direction.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A vector B encodes two things at once: how far (its length, here √(1² + 0.25²) ≈ 1.03) and which way (its direction). Because every point receives the *same* B, relative positions inside the object are unchanged — distances and angles between its points are preserved, which is what 'without distorting it' means.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the geometric reading of the `+ b` in `relu(W @ x + b)`: the bias translates the whole batch of representations by one fixed vector. It is also the first entry in a dictionary (continued on p.61) that maps tensor operations to geometric moves.
paragraphs.technical_idea: For an object given as a matrix of points X (one point per row), the translation is `X + B`, which relies on broadcasting B over every row (p.55).

terminology.meaning: A set of points in the plane treated as one shape (the K in figure 2.9).
Moving every point of an object by the same vector, without distortion.

paragraphs.what_it_says: (Merged with 'and so on, can be expressed as tensor operations' and 'Here are a few examples:') Elementary geometric operations — translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, and so on — can all be expressed as tensor operations; a list of examples follows.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The claim of p.59 that *all* tensor operations have geometric meaning is now stated in the other direction: the familiar geometric moves each correspond to a tensor operation. Translation is addition; rotation, scaling and skewing turn out to be matrix products (p.61).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It lets you read a neural network — a chain of tensor operations — as a chain of geometric transformations, the viewpoint developed on p.62.

paragraphs.excerpt: Translation—As you just saw, adding a vector to a point will move this point
paragraphs.what_it_says: First example: adding a vector to a point moves it by a fixed amount in a fixed direction; applied to a set of points such as a 2-D object, this is a 'translation' (figure 2.9).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Figure 2.9 makes it concrete: the red K is a set of points `[x, y]`; adding `[horizontal_factor, vertical_factor]` to each gives the shifted K. The dashed lines in the figure mark the horizontal and vertical components of the displacement.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Translation is the simplest geometric operation and the one implemented by tensor *addition* — the only geometric operation that is not a matrix product.
paragraphs.technical_idea: $\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} \text{horizontal\_factor} \\ \text{vertical\_factor} \end{pmatrix}$ for every point of the object.

terminology.meaning: The two components of the translation vector in figure 2.9 — how far right and how far up every point moves.

connections: p.59: A + B as a single point moved.
p.61: affine transform = linear transform + translation.

concepts.name: Translation (vector addition)
concepts.definition: Moving every point of an object by the same vector, so the object is copied to a new location without distortion.
concepts.intuition: Slide a sticker across a page: it keeps its shape, only its position changes.
concepts.technical: Point-wise: p' = p + t. For an object stored as a matrix X (points as rows), X + t via broadcasting. Distance and direction of the move are given by t.
concepts.significance: Tensor addition's geometric meaning; the bias term of a Dense layer is a translation of the representation space.
concepts.example: Figure 2.9: the K shifted by [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor]; figure 2.8: A moved by B to A + B.
concepts.misconception: That adding a vector rotates or stretches the object. It only moves it; all internal distances and angles are preserved.

concepts.name: Geometric interpretation of tensor operations
concepts.definition: Reading tensor contents as point coordinates so that tensor operations become geometric transformations; conversely, elementary geometric operations (translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, …) are expressible as tensor operations.
concepts.intuition: Numbers are positions; operations are moves.
concepts.technical: Translation ↔ vector addition (this page); rotation, scaling, linear and affine transforms ↔ matrix products and their combination with addition (p.61).
concepts.significance: Foundation for viewing a neural network as a chain of geometric transformations (p.62).
concepts.misconception: That only 2-D pictures count. The same statements hold in any number of dimensions.

concepts.name: Vector addition (parallelogram picture)
concepts.definition: A + B is reached by chaining B after A (or A after B); the two chains form a parallelogram with A + B at the far corner.
concepts.intuition: Two routes to the same destination.
concepts.technical: Coordinate-wise addition; commutative, which is why figure 2.8 closes into a parallelogram.
concepts.significance: The geometric core of translation and of every bias term.
concepts.misconception: That A + B lies between A and B. It lies beyond both, at the opposite corner of the parallelogram.

deeper.title: Translating a whole object with one broadcast addition
deeper.body:
The text says translation is 'the same vector addition' applied to a group of points. In NumPy that is literally one line, thanks to broadcasting (p.55):

```python
import numpy as np
K = np.array([[1., 0.], [2., 0.], [2., 1.], [1., 1.]])   # corners of a square 'object'
t = np.array([1.5, 0.5])                                # [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor]
K_moved = K + t                                          # every row shifted by t
```

`K_moved` is `[[2.5, 0.5], [3.5, 0.5], [3.5, 1.5], [2.5, 1.5]]` — the same square, elsewhere. Pairwise distances are unchanged, confirming 'without distorting it'. (AI-written code; the idea is the book's.)

deeper.title: Why translation preserves shape
deeper.body:
1. Take any two points p and q of the object.
2. After translation they become p + t and q + t.
3. Their difference is (p + t) − (q + t) = p − q — unchanged.
4. Hence every distance and every angle inside the object is preserved; only the position changes.
5. This is exactly what the authors mean by 'moving the object without distorting it'. (Beyond the book: operations that preserve all distances are called rigid motions or isometries; rotation on p.61 is another.)

deeper.title: The bias as a translation
deeper.body: In `output = relu(matmul(input, W) + b)` (p.52), the `+ b` adds one fixed vector to every sample's representation. Reading this page geometrically, the bias translates the entire cloud of sample points by b in representation space — it does not rotate or stretch the cloud (that is what `matmul(…, W)` does, see p.61). The authors make this identification explicit on p.61 when they call the Dense layer an affine transform; the point here is that the translation half of it is already fully explained by figure 2.9.

deeper.title: Moving furniture
deeper.body: Translating an object is like carrying a table across a room: every leg moves the same distance in the same direction, so the table arrives intact. If instead you pushed only one corner, legs would move by different vectors and the table would deform — that is no longer a translation (it would be a shear or scaling, which need a matrix, p.61).

misconceptions.claim: Adding a vector to an object changes its shape.
misconceptions.correction: The page says translation moves the object 'without distorting it'; every point gets the same displacement, so internal distances are preserved.

misconceptions.claim: Only translation can be expressed as a tensor operation.
misconceptions.correction: The text states that translation, rotation, scaling, skewing 'and so on' can all be expressed as tensor operations; the others use matrix products (p.61).

misconceptions.claim: The new location of A after adding B is independent of B's direction.
misconceptions.correction: Both the distance and the direction from A to the new location are determined by B.

misconceptions.claim: Figure 2.9's label means the object is scaled by horizontal_factor and vertical_factor.
misconceptions.correction: The label is [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor] + [x, y] — an addition; the factors are the components of the translation vector, not scaling multipliers (scaling comes on p.61).

questions.question: According to the page, what does tensor addition represent geometrically when applied to all points of an object?
options: Rotating the object about the origin
Scaling the object by a fixed factor
Translating the object — moving it without distortion
Reflecting the object across an axis
questions.answer: Translating the object — moving it without distortion
questions.explanation: The text says tensor addition 'represents the action of translating an object (moving the object without distorting it) by a certain amount in a certain direction'. Rotation and scaling are matrix products (p.61); reflection is not discussed here.

questions.question: What two properties of the move from A to A + B are determined by the vector B?
questions.explanation: The page states the new location's 'distance and direction from the original point A is determined by the vector B'.

questions.question: Figure 2.9 labels the translation as [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor] + [x, y]. If a corner of the K is at (2, 1) and the translation is (1.5, 0.5), where does that corner go? Does the K change size?
questions.answer: (3.5, 1.5); no — every point moves by the same vector, so the size and shape are unchanged.
questions.explanation: Add component-wise: 2 + 1.5 = 3.5 and 1 + 0.5 = 1.5. Because all points receive the same displacement, differences between points are preserved.

questions.question: Why does figure 2.8 form a parallelogram, and what does each grey arrow represent?
questions.answer: Because A + B = B + A: chaining B after A and chaining A after B both end at the same point. Each grey arrow is a copy of A or B translated to the head of the other vector.
questions.explanation: The grey arrows in the figure are the chained (translated) copies of the black arrows from p.59's description; commutativity of addition closes the shape.

questions.question: List the elementary geometric operations the page says can be expressed as tensor operations.
questions.answer: Translation, rotation, scaling, skewing, 'and so on'.
questions.explanation: The page names these four explicitly and begins the list of examples with translation; rotation and scaling follow on p.61.

questions.question: Which tensor operation implements translation?
options: Matrix product with a diagonal matrix
questions.explanation: The Translation bullet says 'adding a vector to a point will move this point by a fixed amount in a fixed direction'. A diagonal-matrix product is scaling (p.61); maximum is relu-like clipping; reshaping rearranges coefficients.

questions.question: Explain in your own words how the + b in a Dense layer relates to figure 2.9. Which part of the layer formula would move the point cloud, and which part would change its shape?
questions.answer: + b adds the same vector to every sample's representation, which is a translation of the whole point cloud (figure 2.9 with b as [horizontal_factor, vertical_factor]); matmul(input, W) is what rotates/scales/skews the cloud (p.61).
questions.explanation: The page explains translation; the identification with the bias is spelled out by the authors on p.61 when they call the Dense layer an affine transform.
